title: Space of Metric Spaces
notes: Open by making the chapter question concrete: the objects being compared may not have the same points, topology, or visible dimension. The lecture asks what it means for a circle, a finite net, a sphere with a shrinking handle, and a distance table to live near one another.

title: Why Compare Different Point Sets?
notes: Use this slide to separate two habits. A map-based comparison expects a named point in one space to have a named partner in the other. Gromov-Hausdorff comparison instead asks whether the distance patterns can be placed near each other after allowing extra or missing sample points.

title: Examples: Cones, Lattices, Handles
notes: Treat the figure as a gallery of failure modes for naive comparison. Blow-ups produce tangent cones, far-away scaling produces asymptotic cones, lattices remember their path metric in a normed limit, and small handles can vanish even though topology has changed.

title: From Uniform Metrics to Flexible Spaces
notes: This is the transition from fixed-set thinking to variable-space thinking. Uniform convergence of metrics is powerful when the underlying set is fixed, but the chapter needs a comparison that tolerates different cardinalities, disappearing pieces, and finite approximations.

title: Lipschitz Distance
notes: Present Lipschitz distance as a relative-error instrument. It is excellent when a homeomorphism is part of the data and every distance should be distorted by a controlled factor. The logarithm turns multiplicative stretch in both directions into an additive nonnegative number.

title: Finite Metric Relabeling Lab
notes: Use the finite distance matrices as the smallest computable model of Lipschitz comparison. Students can inspect how relabeling tries to match every entry, while the recorded value shows that even a tiny finite example already separates relative distortion from ordinary matrix closeness.

title: Why Lipschitz Is Too Strong
notes: Pause on the restrictions before introducing the new metric. Lipschitz distance demands a bi-Lipschitz homeomorphism, so it cannot compare spaces with different topology or cardinality. A near-duplicate point or a collapsing handle is not a small Lipschitz perturbation of the original space.

title: Hausdorff First, Then Gromov-Hausdorff
notes: Build the definition in two steps. Hausdorff distance works after the spaces already sit inside one ambient metric space. Gromov-Hausdorff distance removes the ambient space from the input by allowing all common placements and taking the best Hausdorff comparison.

title: Correspondences Replace Maps
notes: Explain that a correspondence is deliberately more permissive than a function. Every point must appear, but a point may be paired with several points on the other side. This is exactly the structure needed for duplicate samples, collapsed fibers, and finite approximations of continua.

title: Distortion Heatmap
notes: Read the heatmap as a pairwise stress test. A correspondence is judged not by one paired distance, but by the worst discrepancy between two paired pairs. The notebook check records distortion 0.16 and hence the displayed finite Gromov-Hausdorff upper bound 0.08.

title: The Correspondence Formula
notes: State the formula as the computational heart of the chapter. For compact metric spaces, Gromov-Hausdorff distance can be recovered as one half of the best correspondence distortion. This converts an existential embedding definition into finite distance bookkeeping.

title: Epsilon-Isometries
notes: Use epsilon-isometries as the map-shaped version of the same looseness. The map need not be continuous or bijective; it only needs small distortion and an epsilon-dense image. That difference is what lets a finite net approximate an entire compact space.

title: GH Metric on Compact Spaces
notes: Emphasize that compactness is doing real work. After quotienting by isometry, Gromov-Hausdorff distance is a genuine metric on compact metric spaces. The triangle inequality is believable because correspondences can be composed while their distortions add.

title: Finite Nets Approximate Compact Spaces
notes: Make finite nets feel operational rather than auxiliary. At scale epsilon, a compact space can be seen by finitely many representatives, and the inclusion of that net gives a Gromov-Hausdorff error controlled by the net radius. The CSV records the circle bounds used here.

title: Precompactness Through Total Boundedness
notes: Use this slide to connect convergence to a uniform finite-resolution principle. Uniformly bounded diameter prevents spaces from drifting apart, while a shared bound on epsilon-net sizes prevents uncontrolled small-scale complexity. The diagonal proof then extracts limiting finite distance tables.

title: Limits of Length Spaces
notes: Shift from compactness of the universe to preservation of path geometry. Graph approximations show how sampled shortest-path metrics approach length behavior. The theorem says complete Gromov-Hausdorff limits of compact length spaces remain length spaces because approximate midpoints survive.

title: Midpoint Criterion Proof Flow
notes: Close with the proof mechanism. Choose nearby representatives in approximating length spaces, take an approximate midpoint there, and send it back across a low-distortion correspondence. Letting the error shrink supplies approximate midpoints in the limit, which triggers the midpoint criterion.
